body:
Where Geothermal Resources Are Found

Geothermal resources are unevenly distributed. Regions with favourable geological structures, faults, geothermal gradients and accessible underground fluids are particularly important for exploration. Volcanic and tectonically active regions often provide significant opportunities, but geothermal prospects can also occur in sedimentary basins and other geological settings.

India has several recognised geothermal provinces. Important examples include the Himalayan region, the Son Narmada Tapi (SONATA) region and the Cambay Graben, along with other provinces identified through geological assessment.

Important Indian Locations

Location or regionState or regionSignificance
Puga ValleyLadakhProminent geothermal exploration and demonstration site
ManikaranHimachal PradeshKnown for natural hot springs and direct heat use
Cambay GrabenGujaratRecognised geothermal province associated with basin geology
SONATA regionCentral IndiaRecognised geothermal province linked to major geological structures

Gujarat connection: The Cambay Graben is a recognised geothermal province. This indicates geological resource potential, not proof that a large commercial geothermal electricity industry is already operating there.

National Resource Assessment and Its Meaning

A Press Information Bureau backgrounder dated 2 November 2026 reported that the Geological Survey of India had mapped 381 hot springs and identified 10 geothermal provinces. It also cited nearly 10.6 GW of theoretical geothermal potential and 42 promising sites for power generation or direct heat use.

These figures describe resource assessment and theoretical potential as reported on 2 November 2026. They are not installed electricity-generation capacity, and the figures do not establish that every identified site is commercially viable.

National Policy and Development Status

India notified its National Policy on Geothermal Energy in September 2025, with MNRE serving as the nodal ministry. The policy provides a framework for exploration, resource development and applications of geothermal energy.

In July 2026, the ONGC Energy Centre commissioned 2 geothermal wells at Puga Valley in Ladakh. Each was approximately 1,000 metres deep. These wells were intended to support reservoir evaluation and a prospective 1 MW demonstration geothermal power project.

As reported in the 2 November 2026 government backgrounder, this represented progress in exploration and demonstration. Commissioning exploration wells must not be confused with commissioning a fully operating commercial geothermal power station.

Environmental and Operational Constraints

Geothermal projects generally avoid fuel combustion during normal electricity production, but environmental impacts remain possible. These include:

  • Water and mineral management: Geothermal water may contain dissolved salts, minerals or gases and requires appropriate handling.
  • Air emissions: Some geothermal fluids release gases such as hydrogen sulphide.
  • Land and water effects: Poorly managed extraction may contribute to subsidence, changes in underground pressure or groundwater concerns.
  • Induced seismicity: Some activities that alter underground fluid pressure or fracture pathways can trigger small earthquakes, especially where enhanced geothermal techniques are used.
  • Reservoir sustainability: Excessive heat extraction or inadequate reinjection can reduce local resource performance.

Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) attempt to make heat in suitable underground rock more accessible by improving fluid circulation through engineered pathways. They may expand the range of usable resources but require additional technical and environmental safeguards.

Prelims focus

  • Puga Valley is in Ladakh; Manikaran is in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Cambay Graben is a recognised geothermal province in Gujarat.
  • SONATA stands for Son Narmada Tapi.
  • India notified the National Policy on Geothermal Energy in September 2025.
  • The government reported 381 mapped hot springs and 10 geothermal provinces on 2 November 2026.
  • Trap: A theoretical resource estimate, exploration well or proposed demonstration plant is not the same as installed commercial generating capacity.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, 'Geothermal Energy: A New Chapter in India's Clean Energy Journey', 2 November 2026, sections 'India's Geothermal Resource Base' and 'India's Geothermal Expansion'; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed pp. 35–36; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Geothermal Electricity Generation', accessed 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Seven stages separate geothermal identification from commercial power; India's mapped resources and Puga's assessment wells do not establish commercial generation.
pictures.caption: Geological prospects progress through several stages before commercial electricity generation.

title: Geothermal Resources in India and Gujarat: Locations, Development and Impacts

body:
What Produces Tides?

Tides are periodic variations in sea level, mainly caused by the gravitational influence of the Moon and the Sun together with the motion of the Earth–Moon system. The Moon has the stronger tide-generating influence because it is much closer to Earth.

At many locations, sea level rises and falls approximately twice during a lunar day. However, actual tidal patterns differ between coasts. Some locations experience mainly 2 high tides and 2 low tides each day, others experience mainly 1 of each, and some have mixed patterns. Coastline shape, water depth and basin characteristics modify the tidal range and timing.

Tidal range is the vertical difference in sea level between high tide and low tide. A larger tidal range can provide more favourable conditions for tidal-range power generation, subject to geography and environmental constraints.

Spring Tides and Neap Tides

The changing positions of the Sun, Moon and Earth influence the strength of tides.

  • Spring tides: Occur around new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are approximately aligned. Their gravitational tide-generating effects reinforce one another, generally producing a greater tidal range.
  • Neap tides: Occur around the first-quarter and third-quarter phases of the Moon, when the tide-generating influences of the Sun and Moon partly oppose each other. They generally produce a smaller tidal range.

A spring tide is not a tide occurring only during the spring season. The term refers to a generally greater tidal range. Similarly, a neap tide does not mean that the sea remains at low tide throughout the day.

How Tidal Energy Is Converted into Electricity

Tidal power uses either the difference in water levels or the movement of tidal currents.

Tidal Barrage

A tidal barrage is a barrier built across a suitable estuary or coastal inlet. Water is allowed to move between the sea and an enclosed basin as the tide rises and falls. When a useful difference in water level develops, water passes through turbines and generates electricity.

The barrage approach is most suitable where coastal geography can create a significant tidal range and an appropriate basin. It is not suitable along every coastline.

Tidal-Stream Turbine

A tidal-stream turbine extracts energy from moving tidal water. Its underwater rotor turns in the current and drives a generator. Unlike a barrage, it does not require the enclosure of an entire tidal basin.

Tidal Lagoon

A tidal lagoon uses an enclosed coastal water area to capture energy from differences in tidal water levels. It is related in principle to tidal-range generation but differs from a barrage that closes an existing estuary.

Predictable Does Not Mean Continuous

The timing of tides can be predicted with considerable accuracy. This is useful when planning energy generation. Nevertheless, the speed and direction of tidal currents and the difference between high and low water change throughout the tidal cycle. A tidal plant cannot be assumed to generate its full output continuously.

India and Gujarat: Major Resource Locations

India's Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh in Gujarat are important locations identified for tidal-energy potential. Suitable inlets and coastal conditions can support substantial tidal movement or range.

A Ministry of New and Renewable Energy announcement dated 22 August 2019 identified potential tidal-resource locations in the Khambhat and Kachchh regions. The announcement estimated approximately 12,455 MW of identified tidal-energy potential for India. That was a resource estimate published in 2019, not an installed-capacity figure.

The same announcement clarified that energy from tidal, wave, ocean thermal and other specified ocean-energy sources would be considered renewable energy, including for the then-applicable non-solar Renewable Purchase Obligation framework, which required obligated entities such as electricity distribution companies to meet specified minimum non-solar renewable-electricity targets.

Environmental Concerns

Large tidal barrages can alter water exchange, sediment movement, salinity, intertidal habitats and fish migration. Tidal-stream turbines may create local effects on marine animals and underwater conditions. These impacts depend on the particular technology and site.

Prelims focus

  • Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravitational influence, with a contribution from the Sun.
  • Spring tides generally occur around new moon and full moon.
  • Neap tides generally occur around the first-quarter and third-quarter Moon.
  • A tidal barrage uses a difference in water level; a tidal-stream turbine uses moving water.
  • The Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kachchh are important tidal-resource regions of Gujarat.
  • Trap: The 2019 estimate of 12,455 MW represents identified tidal potential, not installed tidal generating capacity.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 'Water', printed pp. 33–36, especially the explanation of tides and spring/neap tides; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed p. 36; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Press Information Bureau announcement on recognising ocean energy as renewable energy, 22 August 2019, sections 'Potential' and 'Tidal Energy'; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Marine Energy Basics', accessed 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Spring tides near new and full moons have greater tidal range; neap tides near quarter moons have smaller range.
pictures.caption: Moon phases help explain changes in tidal range.

pictures.alt: A barrage uses different sea and basin water levels; a tidal-stream rotor uses moving currents without enclosing the basin. Both generate electricity.

title: Tidal Energy: Gravitational Forces, Spring and Neap Tides, and Power Generation

body:
Why Ocean Waves Contain Energy

Wave energy is the energy associated with the motion of waves on the sea surface. Most ordinary ocean waves form because wind transfers energy to water. The height, period and direction of waves depend on wind conditions, the distance over which wind blows and other characteristics of the sea.

Waves can travel beyond the region where they were generated. Thus, a coast may receive energetic waves even when the local wind is relatively weak.

The energy in waves is different from tidal energy. Ordinary wind-generated waves are not caused primarily by the Moon's gravity. A tsunami is also different: it may result from a sudden disturbance such as an undersea earthquake and is not the normal wind-driven wave resource considered for wave-energy converters.

Basic Wave-Energy Technologies

DeviceWhat moves or changesHow energy is captured
Point absorberFloating or submerged structure moves in response to wavesRelative movement drives a conversion mechanism
Oscillating water columnWaves raise and lower water inside a chamberChanging air pressure drives an air turbine
Overtopping deviceWaves carry water into an elevated reservoirStored water flows back through a turbine
Wave-surge converterA flap or other surface oscillates under wave actionMechanical motion is converted into useful power

The Oscillating Water Column Distinction

An oscillating water column contains air above water inside a chamber. As incoming waves make the water level rise and fall, the air above it is alternately compressed and drawn back. This moving air passes through a turbine to generate electricity.

This distinction is useful because the turbine in such a device is driven by airflow generated by wave motion, rather than necessarily being struck directly by moving seawater.

Ocean Current Energy

Ocean currents are sustained movements of seawater. Surface currents are strongly influenced by winds, while deeper circulation also depends on water temperature, salinity and density differences. The Earth's rotation and the shape of ocean basins influence current patterns.

A marine-current turbine can generate electricity from moving water by using the current to turn a rotor connected to a generator. However, a large-scale ocean current and a reversing local tidal current are not identical phenomena.

Location and Technology Maturity

Wave-energy systems require a sufficiently useful wave climate. The most suitable sites have favourable wave conditions, practical access and manageable environmental risks. Locations exposed to powerful waves may offer more energy but also impose greater demands on the equipment during storms.

Compared with conventional biomass combustion or established geothermal electricity generation, wave-energy technology remains less commercially mature. Many designs have been tested through research and pilot or demonstration deployments, while widespread large-scale commercial deployment remains limited.

Environmental Effects

Potential impacts include disturbance of seabed habitats during installation, underwater noise, interaction with marine animals, changes to local wave conditions and conflicts with fishing or navigation. Marine equipment also faces corrosion, biofouling and damage from extreme weather.

These concerns do not imply that every wave-energy device causes severe damage. Environmental effects depend on its location, design, scale and operation.

Prelims focus

  • Most ordinary ocean waves originate from wind acting on the sea surface.
  • A point absorber uses motion caused by passing waves.
  • An oscillating water column uses wave-induced airflow to drive a turbine.
  • An overtopping device uses water collected in an elevated reservoir.
  • Ocean current energy uses moving seawater; tidal currents are a particular periodic form of water movement.
  • Trap: A tsunami is not an ordinary wind-generated wave and is not a routine tidal-energy resource.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 'Water', printed pp. 33–36, sections 'Waves' and 'Ocean Currents'; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Marine Energy Glossary', sections 'Wave' and 'Current', accessed 16 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Marine Energy Basics', accessed 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Wave-energy devices convert different kinds of motion into useful power.

title: Wave Energy and Ocean Currents: Working Principles and Environmental Constraints
